title: AI Algorithm Detects Hypertension and Diabetes From a Five-Second Facial Video
excerpt: Japanese researchers demonstrate a machine-learning tool that screens for high blood pressure and diabetes using spectroscopic camera footage of the face, no cuffs or blood tests required.
body:
• A machine-learning algorithm detected hypertension with 95% accuracy from a 30-second facial video and 90.3% from just five seconds
  • The same system detected diabetes with 88.2% accuracy from a 30-second recording, using facial blood-flow patterns
  • Developed at the University of Tokyo and Institute of Science Tokyo, the tool could enable contactless screening without cuffs, blood tests, or clinic visits
  • The research was presented at ESC Congress 2026 in Munich and still requires validation in larger, more diverse populations

A brief video of your face may soon be enough to screen for two of the world's most common chronic diseases. Researchers at the University of Tokyo and Institute of Science Tokyo have developed a machine-learning algorithm that can detect hypertension and diabetes from spectroscopic camera footage of the face — with a recording as short as five seconds.

The findings, presented at the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) Congress 2026 in Munich on August 26, point toward a future where smartphone-based health screening could reach populations that never make it to a clinic.

How the Technology Works

The system uses a high-speed spectroscopic camera to record video of a participant's face and palms at 150 frames per second. The algorithm then extracts data on pulse-wave dynamics — which reflect arterial stiffness — along with skin blood-flow patterns and spectral characteristics of skin colouring. These markers are fed into a machine-learning model trained to distinguish between healthy individuals and those with hypertension or diabetes.

In a prospective study of 215 participants, including both diagnosed patients and healthy volunteers, the algorithm detected hypertension with 95.0% accuracy from a 30-second facial and palm video. Sensitivity for identifying normal blood pressure was 100%, while hypertension sensitivity reached 89.2%. Even with just five seconds of footage, accuracy remained at 90.3%.

Diabetes Detection and Blood Pressure Estimation

In newer work building on the hypertension findings, the algorithm was tested for diabetes detection using facial blood-flow patterns alone. It achieved 88.2% accuracy from a 30-second video and 81.2% from a five-second clip.

The system also estimated blood pressure without a cuff, recording a mean absolute percentage error of 8.6% for systolic readings. The mean error of −2.6 mmHg fell within the Association for the Advancement of Medical Instrumentation's acceptable range, though the standard deviation of ±12.0 mmHg exceeded the recommended threshold. The research team said future work would focus on reducing variability through larger, multi-centre datasets.

"If validated, this contactless approach could allow people to be screened in everyday settings — without cuffs, blood sampling or a dedicated clinic visit."

— Ryoko Uchida, University of Tokyo

Why It Matters for Global Health

Approximately 1.4 billion adults worldwide have hypertension and 589 million live with diabetes, according to ESC data. Many cases remain undiagnosed because current screening requires dedicated clinical visits or wearable devices. A contactless tool that works from a brief video could dramatically expand screening capacity, particularly in regions with limited healthcare infrastructure.

"It is remarkable that AI-supported technologies are enabling the development of such powerful tools for early disease prevention," said Nico Bruining, programme co-chair of the ESC Digital and AI Summit. "Because this approach is quick, easy and contactless, it could be used in many settings beyond hospitals."

South Asian Health Implications

The technology holds particular relevance for South Asian populations, who face elevated rates of both hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Studies have consistently shown that people of South Asian descent develop cardiovascular disease at younger ages and lower BMI thresholds than other populations. A low-cost, contactless screening method could help identify at-risk individuals earlier, especially among diaspora communities where routine health checks may be inconsistent.

Limitations and What's Next

The study was single-centre with 215 participants, all recruited in Japan. The research team acknowledged the need for validation across more diverse populations and larger cohorts before real-world deployment. The blood pressure estimation, while promising, exceeded standard accuracy thresholds on variability.

The ESC Congress also featured a separate AI breakthrough: an algorithm developed at Imperial College London that analyses electrocardiogram results at "superhuman" speed, detecting heart failure with up to 81% accuracy and heart valve disease at 90%. That tool is already being trialled in NHS hospitals in London and Bristol.

Both technologies signal a shift toward AI-powered screening that could move cardiovascular and metabolic disease detection out of specialised clinics and into everyday life. The facial video tool, funded by the Japan Science and Technology Agency, is expected to enter larger validation studies in the coming months.
